analysis.one_liner: Adds dental, vision, and hearing coverage to Medicare.
analysis.headline: The bill adding dental, vision, and hearing coverage to Medicare has 131 Democratic cosponsors but has seen no action in committee since its March 2025 introduction.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would add dental, vision, and hearing care to Medicare, which currently does not cover routine cleanings, fillings, dentures, eyeglasses, or hearing aids. Coverage would start in 2026 for preventive dental services and phase in more fully through 2029, with seniors paying 20% coinsurance and modest limits on items like eyeglasses and hearing aids. It has 131 Democratic cosponsors but has not moved in the two committees it was referred to.
analysis.who_benefits: People on Medicare — about 67 million seniors and disabled Americans — would gain coverage for care Medicare has historically excluded: cleanings, fillings, crowns, root canals, dentures, routine eye exams, eyeglasses and contact lenses, and hearing exams and hearing aids [S2][S3]. Low-income beneficiaries would get fuller coverage faster, with basic dental services covered at 80% starting in 2027 rather than phased in through 2029 [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Medicare would cover preventive and basic dental care starting in 2026, with basic and major services phasing in to 80% payment by 2029, and full payment for low-income beneficiaries starting 2027
It would cover dentures, which Medicare has excluded since the program's creation, at 80% payment with one set every five years
It would cover annual routine eye exams, eyeglass lenses and frames up to $100 each, contact lenses up to $200 per two years with inflation adjustments, and low vision devices
It would cover routine hearing exams and hearing aids at 80% payment, with one hearing aid per ear every four years

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, through higher Medicare spending, and Medicare beneficiaries, who would still pay 20% coinsurance on most of these services (with limits like $100 per pair of eyeglass lenses and one hearing aid per ear every four years) [S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill does not identify a funding source for the new benefit, so it would add to federal Medicare spending — an honest supporter would have to say how it is paid for
Coverage is limited and phased in: eyeglass lenses and frames are capped at $100 each, contact lenses at $200 per two years, and full payment for most dental services is not reached until 2029
The Secretary of Health and Human Services is given broad authority to impose prior authorization and other limits, which could narrow the benefit in practice

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real and addresses a well-known gap: Medicare covers hospital stays and doctors but not the teeth, eyes, and ears problems that most burden older adults, and out-of-pocket dental costs are the most common care seniors skip. The main cost is federal spending with no dedicated funding source in the bill, plus dollar caps on glasses and hearing aids that keep the benefit narrower than the headline. The design is reasonable — phased-in payment rates and Secretary authority to set limits restrain costs — but the caps are stingy enough that low-income seniors would still face meaningful out-of-pocket costs for major dental work.

outcome.mechanism: The bill has sat in two House committees since it was introduced in March 2025, with no hearings or votes scheduled.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 11, 2025, and referred the same day to the Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means Committees
No further action has been taken in either committee since referral

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Seniors who need dental, vision, and hearing coverage are no better off yet — the benefit does not exist. The status quo favors the federal budget's bottom line and the companies selling seniors separate dental, vision, and hearing coverage out of pocket.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Seniors awaiting Medicare dental and hearing coverage

for.name: Rep. Lloyd Doggett
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 131 Democratic cosponsors

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 131 cosponsors are House Democrats, and no Republicans have signed on; with Republicans holding 223 House seats, the bill lacks the majority it would need even if it reached the floor.

industries.note: Medicare would become a payer for cleanings, fillings, crowns, and dentures, bringing millions of seniors into dentists' chairs as paying patients. Payment is set at 80% of a Medicare-determined fee, lower than many private rates, but the volume of new covered patients is a large gain.

Hearing aids and hearing exams move from out-of-pocket to Medicare-covered, with one hearing aid per ear every four years paid at 80%. Manufacturers gain a vast new payer base, though Medicare-negotiated rates may be below retail prices.

The bill pays 80% toward glasses and contacts but caps lenses at $100 per year and frames at $100 every two years, so makers of premium eyewear gain less than the coverage headline suggests. Routine eye exams would be covered annually.

industries.industry: Standalone dental and vision insurance sellers
industries.note: Companies selling standalone dental, vision, and hearing plans to seniors would see much of their market absorbed by a public benefit. Their interest lies in keeping these services outside Medicare.

Medicare Advantage plans often tout dental, vision, and hearing extras as their selling point; a universal traditional-Medicare benefit would force them to match it and erase that advantage, while also passing new required costs to their plans.

analysis.trajectory: This kind of bill rarely reaches the House floor: with 131 cosponsors but no committee action months after referral and no Republican support, the likely path is that it stays in committee unless health care becomes part of a larger budget or reconciliation package in which dental, vision, and hearing coverage is negotiated in.
